intervention_label: HA-1 TCR-T (donor-derived CD8+/CD4+ memory T cells, Bleakley/HighPassBio platform)
model_system: human primary CD4+ and CD8+ memory T cells lentivirally transduced with the HA-1 TCR transgene; cytotoxicity against primary HLA-A*02:01+ HA-1H+ leukemia blasts
control_arm: untransduced and irrelevant-TCR-transduced T cells from the same donors; HA-1-negative and HLA-A2-negative targets
mechanism: An HLA-A*02:01-restricted TCR against HA-1H, a minor histocompatibility antigen whose expression is confined to haematopoietic tissue, so donor-derived T cells kill recipient leukaemia without the broad tissue toxicity of unselected alloreactivity. The transgene also carries a CD8 coreceptor (to make the class-I TCR work in CD4+ cells), an inducible caspase-9 kill switch, and a CD34-CD20 selection/tracking epitope.
key_finding: Both CD4+ and CD8+ transduced memory T cells recognised and killed primary HA-1H-positive leukaemia; naive T cells were excluded from the product to limit native-TCR alloreactivity. This is the construct behind NCT03326921, so the preclinical package and the trial product are the same object.
caveats: In-vitro human work only — no xenograft efficacy arm in this paper. Applicability here is entirely conditional on retrieving HLA-A*02:01 status plus recipient HA-1(H)-positive / sibling-donor HA-1-negative genotyping, neither of which is on hand.

intervention_label: HA-1-specific transgenic TCR CD8+ T cells (independent TCR panel)
model_system: CD8+ T cells with endogenous TCR knocked out and one of 13 HA-1-specific transgenic TCRs; cytotoxicity against primary leukaemia cells from HA-1+ patients
n_units: 15 HA-1-positive patient samples (AML, T-ALL, B-ALL); 10 HA-1-negative or HLA-A*02-negative donor controls; 28-allele HLA panel for cross-reactivity
control_arm: cells from HA-1-negative or HLA-A*02:01-negative donors; peripheral blood mononuclear cells across 28 common HLA alleles
mechanism: Transgenic HA-1/HLA-A*02:01 TCRs redirect CD8+ T cells against a haematopoiesis-restricted polymorphic peptide; knocking out the endogenous TCR removes mispairing and raises transgenic TCR surface density.
key_finding: Lysis occurred against haematopoietic cells from HA-1-positive patients including AML, and was absent against HA-1-negative or HLA-A*02-negative donors. No cross-reactivity appeared across a 28-allele HLA panel.
caveats: In vitro only, with reporter-line affinity ranking rather than in-vivo efficacy. Independent replication of the HA-1 target rather than of the specific TSC-100 or HighPassBio product.

intervention_label: HA-2-directed TCR gene transfer (mechanism basis for the HA-2 arm, e.g. TSC-101)
model_system: peripheral T lymphocytes from HLA-A2-positive HA-2-negative and from HLA-A2-negative donors, retrovirally transduced with HA-2-specific TCR alpha/beta pairs; cytotoxicity against HA-2-expressing leukaemia targets
control_arm: mock-transduced T cells; HA-2-negative targets; chimeric TCR variants dissecting the Jalpha42 and CDR3 contributions
mechanism: Transfer of a TCR against HA-2, a second haematopoiesis-restricted minor histocompatibility antigen presented by HLA-A2, converts unselected donor T cells into leukaemia-reactive effectors.
key_finding: Thirteen HA-2-specific clones shared a conserved Jalpha42 segment, and TCRs transferred into HA-2-negative donor T cells produced antileukaemic lysis. Transfer into HLA-A2-negative donor T cells preserved antileukaemic activity without anti-HLA-A2 alloreactivity.
caveats: Twenty-three-year-old retroviral work, in vitro only, and the TCR is not the one in TSC-101. The HA-2 arm of the current clinical programme rests on a thinner and older preclinical base than the HA-1 arm.

intervention_label: Genomic HLA haplotype loss as a post-transplant escape route
exclusion_reason: The escape mechanism it describes — acquired uniparental disomy of 6p deleting the donor-mismatched HLA haplotype — needs a mismatched haplotype to delete. This patient's graft came from an HLA-identical sibling, so there is no mismatched haplotype for the leukaemia to lose, and the finding does not carry over to her late relapse.

intervention_label: WT1-siTCR gene-transduced lymphocytes (TBI-1301, HLA-A*24:02-restricted)
model_system: human T cells transduced with a retroviral WT1-specific TCR vector carrying siRNAs against endogenous TCR chains; autologous primary leukaemia killing plus a mouse xenograft leukaemia model
control_arm: conventional codon-optimised WT1 TCR (WT1-coTCR) transduced T cells; normal CD34+ haematopoietic progenitors as an on-target/off-tumour readout
mechanism: siRNA silencing of the endogenous TCR alpha and beta chains suppresses mispairing and raises surface expression of the introduced WT1/HLA-A*24:02 TCR, which increases avidity for WT1 peptide on leukaemia cells.
key_finding: siTCR-transduced T cells outperformed the conventional WT1 TCR construct, lysed autologous patient leukaemia while sparing normal haematopoietic progenitors, and controlled leukaemia in xenografted mice without inhibiting human haematopoiesis. Repeated WT1-peptide stimulation expanded the cells without loss of specificity.
caveats: Restriction is HLA-A*24:02, so this arm only opens if the pending typing returns A*24:02 — it is the fallback if A*02:01 is negative, not a parallel option.

intervention_label: WT1-specific TCR-redirected CD4+ T cells (class-I-restricted TCR in CD4 compartment)
exclusion_reason: In-vitro characterisation of CD4+ helper function from the same laboratory; the CD4-augmentation argument it makes is already carried, in the product actually on the trial list, by the CD8-coreceptor design in Dossa 2018.

intervention_label: MDG1011 (PRAME-directed, HLA-A*02:01-restricted autologous TCR-T)
model_system: preclinical MDG1011 batches from enriched CD8+ T cells of healthy donors, plus 13 patient-derived investigational medicinal products; on-target and off-target panels of tumour and healthy-tissue test cells
n_units: 2 preclinical batches; 13 patient IMPs (manufacturing success 92%); 9 IMPs administered
control_arm: healthy-tissue test cell panels for on-target/off-tumour and off-target screening
mechanism: A recombinant TCR against the PRAME100-108 VLD peptide on HLA-A*02:01 redirects autologous CD8+ T cells to PRAME-expressing myeloid blasts; PRAME is largely absent from normal adult tissue outside testis.
key_finding: Batches expressed the VLD-TCR at high density and produced antigen-specific IFN-gamma and cytotoxicity with no signal of on-target/off-tumour or off-target recognition. Manufacturing succeeded in 12 of 13 heavily pretreated patients, which is the practical question for a patient at 85% marrow blasts.
caveats: No animal efficacy arm and no leukaemia-burden endpoint; specificity and manufacturability are the endpoints. PRAME expression on this patient's blasts has not been measured, and the target validator logged PRAME as not assessable.

intervention_label: CG1/HLA-A2 x CD3 TCR-mimetic bispecific T-cell engager (preclinical basis for CBX-250)
model_system: HLA-A2-positive primary AML blasts and AML cell lines in vitro, plus in-vivo AML models; normal bone marrow as the toxicity comparator
control_arm: HLA-A2-negative leukaemia targets; normal bone marrow; T cells without engager
mechanism: Cathepsin G is an azurophil-granule protease expressed more highly in AML blasts than in normal myeloid progenitors; its leader-sequence peptide CG1 is preferentially loaded onto HLA-A*02:01. A TCR-mimetic antibody against the CG1/HLA-A2 complex, formatted as a CD3 bispecific, recruits polyclonal T cells to that complex.
key_finding: The engager bound CG1/HLA-A2 monomers with high affinity and killed HLA-A2-positive primary AML and cell lines both in vitro and in vivo, with T-cell activation and cytokine release tracking tumour and drug exposure. No activity was seen against normal bone marrow.
caveats: Gated on HLA-A*02:01, which is unresolved here; CG1/HLA-A2 surface density on this patient's blasts is also unmeasured and has no routine assay. Crossbow Therapeutics co-authors, so read the safety margin with sponsor involvement in mind.

intervention_label: CG1/HLA-A2 TCR-mimetic CAR T cells
model_system: CG1/A2 TCR-mimic scFv-based CAR T cells against HLA-A2-positive AML and CML lines and primary samples, in vitro and in vivo; normal bone marrow haematopoiesis as safety readout
control_arm: untransduced T cells; HLA-A2-negative targets; normal bone marrow colony assays
mechanism: The same CG1/HLA-A2 TCR-mimic binder rebuilt as a CAR ectodomain, so recognition of a peptide-HLA complex drives CAR signalling rather than antibody-mediated T-cell recruitment.
key_finding: CG1/A2-CAR T cells killed HLA-A2-positive AML and CML in vitro and in vivo and left normal bone marrow haematopoiesis intact. The two formats together make the case that the CG1/A2 complex, not the format, is the discriminating element.
caveats: A different modality from the CD3 engager on the trial list, so it corroborates the antigen rather than the product. Same laboratory and same binder as Shi 2025, so the two are not independent replication.

intervention_label: Pivekimab sunirine (IMGN632, CD123-directed antibody-drug conjugate)
model_system: AML cell lines and patient-derived AML samples in culture; normal human myeloid progenitors; multiple AML xenograft models
control_arm: X-ADC, the same G4723A antibody carrying a DNA-crosslinking IGN payload; unconjugated antibody; normal bone marrow progenitors
mechanism: A humanised anti-CD123 antibody delivers a DNA mono-alkylating indolinobenzodiazepine pseudodimer. Swapping the crosslinking payload for a mono-alkylator is what buys the therapeutic window, since crosslinking IGNs are far more toxic to normal progenitors.
key_finding: Both conjugates reduced AML viability at low picomolar concentrations irrespective of multidrug-resistance phenotype or disease status, but the crosslinking comparator was more than 40-fold more toxic to normal myeloid progenitors than IMGN632. Antitumour activity held across several AML xenograft models.
caveats: Sponsor-run study (ImmunoGen). Relapsed/refractory post-transplant disease and extramedullary sites are not represented in the model set.

intervention_label: Pivekimab sunirine — determinants of response (CD123 density, TP53, BCL-2 family)
model_system: 13 human acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukaemia cell lines, isogenic TP53-knockout/parental pairs, sublines overexpressing BCL-2, BCL-xL or MCL-1, and 9 primary AML samples
n_units: 13 cell lines; 5 isogenic TP53-KO/parental pairs; 9 primary AML samples
control_arm: parental TP53 wild-type lines; non-overexpressing parental sublines; unconjugated antibody and free payload
mechanism: After CD123-mediated internalisation the IGN payload alkylates DNA, and the resulting death signal runs through a p53-dependent, BCL-2-family-gated apoptotic pathway — so both antigen density at the front end and apoptotic competence at the back end set the response.
key_finding: Cytotoxicity tracked CD123 expression (R2=0.4469, P=0.0125), was significantly lower in TP53-knockout cells than in the matched wild-type parents across all 5 isogenic pairs, and was reduced in sublines overexpressing BCL-2 or BCL-xL. Three of the case's open variables — CD123 density, TP53 status, and prior venetoclax failure — are exactly the three modifiers this study identifies.
caveats: Published as a short letter with no in-vivo arm, and the R2 of 0.45 means antigen density explains under half the variance. TP53 knockout is a clean genetic model, not the mixed subclonal or copy-loss picture this patient probably has.

intervention_label: CD123-directed CAR T cells — affinity and antigen-density thresholds
model_system: anti-CD123 CAR T cells with structure-guided affinity mutations in the binding domain, tested against AML lines and CD123-low healthy targets across a range of antigen densities
control_arm: parental high-affinity CAR; CAR-negative T cells; CD123-low normal endothelium and progenitor targets
mechanism: CAR output is set by the product of binding affinity, CAR surface expression and target antigen density; lowering affinity raises the antigen threshold needed to trigger a response, which is how on-target/off-tumour recognition of CD123-low normal tissue can be dialled down.
key_finding: Early cytotoxicity was largely insensitive to CAR affinity or expression, but later effector functions such as cytokine release and proliferation failed when CAR expression was low. Distinct lytic and activation antigen thresholds emerged, and lowering affinity preserved anti-AML killing while improving the normal-tissue margin.
caveats: In vitro threshold work with no leukaemia-burden endpoint, and the constructs are not the Allo-RevCAR01/R-TM123 system on the trial list. It gives the board a framework for reading the pending quantitative CD123 flow, not a prediction for a specific product.

intervention_label: DT388IL3 (diphtheria toxin-IL-3 fusion; the molecule marketed as tagraxofusp)
model_system: irradiated SCID mice inoculated intravenously, intraperitoneally or subcutaneously with v-SRC-transfected TF1 human AML cells
n_units: n=45 (i.v.), n=20 (i.p.), n=20 (s.c.) control animals; 49 DT388IL3-treated i.v. animals
control_arm: saline; DT388GMCSF; DAB389IL2; cytarabine 80 microg; anti-CD33-calicheamicin conjugate 5 microg
dose_and_schedule: 2 microg DT388IL3 i.p. daily x up to 5 doses, beginning 24 h after tumour inoculation
mechanism: IL-3 fused to the catalytic and translocation domains of diphtheria toxin binds CD123 (IL-3 receptor alpha), internalises, and shuts down protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2 — a cell-kill mechanism that does not route through the apoptotic machinery venetoclax and calicheamicin depend on.
key_finding: Only 5 of 49 intravenously inoculated treated mice died of leukaemia and median disease-free survival exceeded 120 days versus 37 days for controls. The subcutaneous arm behaved very differently: median disease-free survival rose only from 21 to 31 days, so the same dose that near-eradicated disseminated marrow disease barely dented a solid tissue deposit.
caveats: The subcutaneous-versus-intravenous gap is the closest preclinical analogue on hand for this patient's thigh myeloid sarcoma, and it argues against relying on CD123 immunotoxin alone to clear an extramedullary site. A single transfected cell line in SCID mice, published in 2003.

intervention_label: DT388IL3 variant with enhanced IL-3 receptor binding
exclusion_reason: Characterises an affinity-enhanced IL-3 variant that was not the molecule taken forward as tagraxofusp, and the endpoints are receptor binding and in-vitro cytotoxicity rather than leukaemia control.

intervention_label: Flotetuzumab (MGD006, CD123 x CD3 DART) — nonhuman-primate PK/PD
exclusion_reason: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling in healthy cynomolgus monkeys with no leukaemia and no antileukaemic endpoint; the human efficacy question is already answered by the clinical rows for this agent.

intervention_label: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin vs CD33/CD3 BiTE AMG 330 — dependence on CD33 antigen density
model_system: pretreatment primary specimens from 45 adults with AML, assayed ex vivo for CD33 surface density, rs12459419 genotype, and cytotoxicity from gemtuzumab ozogamicin and from AMG 330 with autologous T cells
n_units: n=45 primary AML specimens (rs12459419: CC 31.1%, CT 57.8%, TT 11.1%)
control_arm: drug-free wells; comparison across the two agents on the same specimens
mechanism: An ADC has to internalise enough conjugate to deliver a lethal calicheamicin dose, so surface CD33 acts as a proxy for intracellular payload. A T-cell engager only needs enough antigen to form a functional immune synapse, which is a much lower bar.
key_finding: CD33 density correlated with gemtuzumab ozogamicin cytotoxicity (r2=0.3124, P<0.0001) but not with AMG 330 killing (r2=0.0136, P=0.45 at 100 pg/mL). The rs12459419 genotype shifted CD33 expression roughly ten-fold (CC 2,344+/-579 vs TT 255+/-91 MFI) yet did not by itself predict cytotoxicity for either agent.
caveats: This is the paper that answers how much the pending quantitative CD33 flow actually matters: density is a real but partial determinant for the ADC (about a third of the variance) and close to irrelevant for a T-cell-redirecting format. Ex-vivo cytotoxicity, not patient outcome.

intervention_label: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin combined with BCL-2 and PI3K inhibition
model_system: four AML cell lines of differing phenotype treated with gemtuzumab ozogamicin alone and with selective BCL-2 and/or PI3K inhibition
control_arm: untreated cells; single-agent gemtuzumab ozogamicin; single-agent inhibitors
mechanism: Calicheamicin-induced double-strand breaks trigger the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, which BCL-2 restrains; removing that brake lowers the damage threshold for commitment to apoptosis.
key_finding: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin caused G2/M arrest and apoptosis, but the magnitude varied widely across the four lines and did not track CD33 expression. Adding BCL-2 and/or PI3K inhibition increased the pro-apoptotic response.
caveats: Four cell lines, in vitro only, and its no-correlation-with-CD33 result sits against the 45-specimen correlation in Laszlo 2019 — the small line panel is the more likely explanation. The BCL-2 synergy it reports is less useful here than it looks, since this patient has already progressed through venetoclax.

intervention_label: CD33-directed CAR T cells — construct optimisation (lintuzumab-CD28/CD3zeta)
model_system: six CD33 CAR constructs (three scFvs x CD28 or 4-1BB costimulation) in lentivirally transduced human T cells; CD33+ AML cell lines and childhood AML patient-derived xenografts
n_units: 6 CAR constructs; AML cell line and PDX in-vivo models
control_arm: untransduced T cells; head-to-head comparison across scFv and costimulatory domain
mechanism: The costimulatory endodomain sets CAR T expansion and persistence, and the scFv sets both epitope and tonic signalling — so myeloid-antigen CAR potency and toxicity are construct-dependent rather than antigen-dependent.
key_finding: CD28-based constructs suppressed leukaemia more consistently than 4-1BB-based constructs in both cell-line and PDX models, and lintuzumab-CD28/CD3zeta was carried forward for clinical translation. Gemtuzumab-scFv-based constructs were unexpectedly toxic in vivo despite in-vitro activity, a mismatch worth remembering when in-vitro data are the only data available.
caveats: PDX models are paediatric AML, not post-transplant adult AML-MR, and CD33 CAR T cells carry unresolved myeloablation risk in a patient whose only route to durable control is another graft. Carries a 2021 publisher erratum, not a retraction.

intervention_label: Loop33 x 123 dual CD33/CD123 CAR T cells
model_system: loop-configuration bivalent CAR T cells from healthy-donor T cells; AML cell lines and primary AML cells in coculture; cell-derived xenografts using wild-type MOLM-13 and a mixture of MOLM-13-KO33 and MOLM-13-KO123 as an antigen-escape model
control_arm: monovalent CD33 and CD123 CAR T cells; untransduced T cells
mechanism: A single receptor carrying binders for both CD33 and CD123 fires when either antigen is present, so a blast that has lost one antigen is still recognised through the other.
key_finding: Loop33 x 123 CAR T cells cleared AML lines and primary AML cells with higher degranulation and cytokine output than the monovalent constructs, and controlled the mixed CD33-knockout/CD123-knockout xenograft that single-antigen CARs could not. Loop orientation mattered: the 33 x 123 arrangement outperformed 123 x 33.
caveats: The escape model is engineered knockout rather than the naturally heterogeneous antigen expression expected between this patient's marrow and her thigh sarcoma. No clinical product with this design is on the trial list; the relevant trial is a CLL-1/CD33/CD123 CAR (NCT04010877) with a different architecture.

intervention_label: Second-generation CD33 TriKE (cam1615CD33, the molecule developed as GTB-3650)
model_system: human NK cells with CD33-expressing leukaemia targets in vitro; preclinical mouse tumour-control models
control_arm: first-generation scFv-anti-CD16 TriKE; NK cells alone; IL-15 alone
mechanism: Three arms in one molecule: a humanised single-domain antibody against CD16 to trigger NK activation, an anti-CD33 arm for target recognition, and an IL-15 moiety that drives NK expansion and priming without systemic cytokine exposure. NK-mediated killing does not require HLA presentation, which matters when class I/II escape is on the table.
key_finding: Replacing the anti-CD16 scFv with a single-domain antibody produced stronger and more NK-selective proliferation without T-cell stimulation, higher killing of CD33-expressing targets, and better tumour control in mouse models. Selectivity for NK over T cells is the practical advance.
caveats: Antigen-density dependence was not systematically dissected, so the pending CD33 quantitation cannot be read against these data. NK function in a patient six years past allograft and through FLAG-IDA is unknown.

intervention_label: 211At-anti-CD45 radioimmunotherapy (211At-B10-30F11; the murine analogue of 211At-BC8-B10)
model_system: disseminated murine AML in leukaemic SJL/J mice with syngeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation; biodistribution plus survival
control_arm: 0 microCi (transplant without radioimmunotherapy); dose-titration arms
dose_and_schedule: single injection of 211At-B10-30F11 at 24, 20, 12 or 0 microCi, followed by syngeneic HSCT
mechanism: An alpha emitter conjugated to anti-CD45 puts short-range, high-linear-energy-transfer radiation onto every haematopoietic cell including the leukaemic clone. The short path length confines the dose relative to beta emitters, which is what allows marrow ablation without proportional organ toxicity.
key_finding: Median survival scaled with dose — 123, 101, 61 and 37 days at 24, 20, 12 and 0 microCi. Conjugate localised to marrow and spleen (18% and 79% injected dose per gram at 24 h) with lower kidney and lung uptake, and white cell nadirs stayed above 2.7 K/microL with recovery by four weeks.
caveats: Syngeneic mouse transplant with a murine anti-CD45 antibody, so neither the allogeneic immunology nor the human antibody is modelled. No clinical efficacy data exist for 211At-BC8-B10, which makes this the entire evidence base for that trial option.

intervention_label: Rezatapopt (PC14586) in TP53-Y220C AML — mechanism and combination dependency
model_system: TP53-Y220C AML cell lines and primary patient samples including stem/progenitor fractions; TP53-Y220C AML xenografts
control_arm: vehicle; rezatapopt alone versus rezatapopt plus venetoclax, MDM2 inhibition, or XPO1 inhibition
mechanism: Rezatapopt occupies the crevice created by the Y220C substitution and restores a wild-type p53 conformation, which reactivates p53 transcriptional targets. Two things then blunt the effect: MDM2 induced by the reactivated protein and XPO1-mediated nuclear export both damp transcription, and the refolded protein fails to bind BCL-2, BCL-xL and MCL-1 the way genuine wild-type p53 does — so the transcription-independent apoptotic arm is missing.
key_finding: Rezatapopt converted p53-Y220C to a wild-type conformation and activated p53 targets, but induced limited or no apoptosis on its own in TP53-Y220C AML. Adding venetoclax supplied the missing BCL-2/BAX displacement, producing extensive death of blasts and stem/progenitor cells in vitro and prolonging xenograft survival; MDM2 or XPO1 inhibition restored the transcriptional arm.
caveats: Single-agent effect is weak — the strong readout needs venetoclax, and this patient has already progressed through venetoclax with FLAG-IDA, so the one combination that rescues rezatapopt in these models is the one she has already failed. A confirmed Y220C therefore opens a partial lever, not a clean one; PMV Pharmaceuticals authors and funding.

intervention_label: Rezatapopt — discovery and characterisation of Y220C reactivation
model_system: biochemical and structural analyses of p53-Y220C, in-vitro and in-vivo transcriptomics, and solid-tumour xenograft models as single agent and with immunotherapy
control_arm: vehicle; p53 wild-type and non-Y220C mutant comparators
mechanism: A designed small molecule binds the Y220C-specific surface pocket, corrects protein conformation, and restores sequence-specific DNA binding so the wild-type transcriptional programme reassembles.
key_finding: Conformational correction translated into recovery of multiple arms of the wild-type p53 programme and antitumour activity in preclinical models, alone and combined with immunotherapy. This is the paper that establishes the molecule; it does not test myeloid disease.
caveats: Solid-tumour models throughout, with no AML or MDS system — the leukaemia-specific result, and the apoptotic shortfall it uncovers, comes from Carter 2025 instead. Written by PMV Pharmaceuticals employees.

intervention_label: Eprenetapopt (APR-246/PRIMA-1Met) plus azacitidine in TP53-mutated MDS/AML
model_system: TP53-mutated MDS/AML cell lines, TP53-mutated primary patient cells, and in-vivo models; transcriptomic profiling of treated cells
control_arm: untreated cells; single-agent APR-246; single-agent azacitidine; FLT3-ligand rescue arm
mechanism: APR-246 converts to methylene quinuclidinone, which alkylates cysteines in the mutant p53 core domain and restores transactivation. Combining with azacitidine adds hypomethylation, and the transcriptomic readout points to downregulation of FLT3 signalling as the shared node.
key_finding: Low-dose APR-246 reactivated the p53 pathway and induced apoptosis, synergising with azacitidine in TP53-mutated cell lines, primary MDS/AML cells and in vivo. Adding FLT3 ligand reversed the antiproliferative effect, identifying FLT3 pathway suppression as the mediator of synergy.
caveats: Mechanism is broad mutant-p53 refolding rather than variant-selective, which is why eprenetapopt reads as low-yield here — its randomised clinical programme has already failed its primary endpoint. Applies only if TP53 aberration is confirmed.

intervention_label: XPO1-mediated resistance to eprenetapopt plus azacitidine
model_system: sequential genotyped samples from two phase 2 trials, a genome-wide CRISPR screen in TP53-mutated leukaemia cells, and a patient-derived xenograft of TP53-mutant MDS
control_arm: pretreatment paired samples; eprenetapopt alone; XPO1 inhibitor alone
mechanism: XPO1 is overexpressed after eprenetapopt/azacitidine exposure and exports reactivated p53 out of the nucleus, which is necessary and sufficient for resistance; blocking nuclear export keeps p53 where it can act.
key_finding: A genome-wide CRISPR screen nominated XPO1, and the trial samples confirmed XPO1 overexpression after treatment. Combining eprenetapopt with XPO1 inhibitors overcame resistance across model systems including a TP53-mutant MDS PDX.
caveats: Relapse was near-universal in these trials unless transplant followed — the honest read is that p53 reactivation buys a window for a graft rather than durable control. XPO1 convergence with the Carter 2025 rezatapopt data is worth noting; the same export brake limits both compounds.

intervention_label: Venetoclax / BCL-2 inhibition — TP53-dependent resistance (prior exposure in this case)
model_system: genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 resistance screen in AML cell lines with validation knockouts; cross-referenced against Beat AML patient drug-response and expression data
control_arm: parental unedited lines; non-targeting guides
mechanism: Venetoclax kills by freeing BIM and BAX from BCL-2, so loss of TP53, BAX or PMAIP1 removes the effector machinery downstream of target engagement. Resistant cells also lower BCL2 and lean on BCL2L1, with accompanying shifts in mitochondrial homeostasis and metabolism.
key_finding: TP53, BAX and PMAIP1 knockouts each conferred venetoclax resistance, and resistance was accompanied by reduced BCL2 expression and reliance on alternative family members. TP53-knockout cells gained sensitivity to TRK inhibitors, an unexpected collateral vulnerability.
caveats: This is the most direct mechanistic account of why FLAG-IDA plus venetoclax failed in a TP53-aberrant patient, and it argues against re-treating with a venetoclax backbone. Isogenic knockouts model clean biallelic loss rather than the subclonal or copy-loss pattern likely here.

intervention_label: Venetoclax — monocytic-differentiation resistance and MCL1 dependence
model_system: paired patient specimens across venetoclax/azacitidine response, single-cell and bulk transcriptomics, primary AML subpopulations sorted by developmental phenotype, metabolic and BH3 profiling
control_arm: phenotypically primitive AML populations from the same patients; responders versus non-responders
mechanism: Monocytic AML cells drop BCL2 expression, run oxidative phosphorylation off MCL1 instead, and so survive BCL-2 inhibition; venetoclax then acts as a selection pressure that lets those subclones expand at relapse.
key_finding: Response tracked developmental stage — primitive AML was sensitive and monocytic AML resistant — with resistant cells showing a distinct transcriptome, loss of BCL2, and MCL1-dependent survival. Relapse specimens were enriched for the monocytic subpopulation.
caveats: This patient's blasts are CD34-positive and CD14/CD64-negative, so the monocytic route probably does not explain her venetoclax failure — the TP53/apoptotic-network route in Nechiporuk 2019 fits better. Logged so the board can rule it out on immunophenotype rather than assume it.

intervention_label: Post-transplant AML relapse — MHC class II downregulation as immune escape
model_system: paired presentation/relapse primary AML samples analysed by exome and RNA sequencing, flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry, with in-vitro interferon-gamma treatment of blasts
n_units: 15 patients relapsing after HCT (matched-sibling, matched-unrelated or mismatched-unrelated) vs 20 relapsing after chemotherapy; 34 post-HCT relapses in the extended flow/IHC set
control_arm: relapse after chemotherapy rather than transplant; paired presentation samples from the same patients
mechanism: Selection pressure from donor T cells favours blasts that stop presenting antigen to CD4+ cells; MHC class II genes are transcriptionally downregulated rather than mutated or deleted, which is why exome sequencing misses it.
key_finding: Post-transplant relapse carried no relapse-specific mutations in immune genes, but HLA-DPA1, HLA-DPB1, HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DRB1 fell 3- to 12-fold, and reduced MHC class II protein was confirmed in 17 of 34 post-HCT relapses. Interferon-gamma reversed the phenotype rapidly in vitro.
caveats: The cohort includes matched-sibling grafts, so unlike genomic HLA-haplotype loss this mechanism is available to this patient. It is a class II phenomenon, so it degrades CD4-mediated graft-versus-leukaemia and DLI more than it degrades a class-I-restricted HLA-A*02:01 TCR product.

intervention_label: Post-transplant relapse — CIITA-driven HLA class II loss plus inhibitory ligand upregulation
model_system: purified AML blasts from serial timepoints across the disease history, genomic and expression profiling, validated in two independent patient cohorts with paired circulating donor T-cell phenotyping
control_arm: the same patients' pre-transplant and chemotherapy-relapse timepoints; independent validation cohorts
mechanism: Two separable escape routes converge on losing donor T-cell recognition: downregulation of the class II master regulator CIITA silences HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP, while PD-L1, B7-H3, CD80 and PVRL2 rise to deliver inhibitory signals. Interferon-gamma reverses the first, checkpoint blockade the second.
key_finding: A transcriptional signature specific to post-transplant relapse was heavily enriched for T-cell costimulation and antigen presentation, with coordinated changes in circulating donor T cells. Loss of class II expression and upregulation of inhibitory checkpoints behaved as alternative, largely non-overlapping escape modalities.
caveats: Overlaps substantially with Christopher 2018 — kept because it adds the CIITA mechanism, the checkpoint-ligand arm, and the pharmacological reversal that make the interferon-gamma plus DLI trial option (NCT06529731) mechanistically coherent for this patient.

intervention_label: PRC2 inhibition to restore HLA class II and rebuild donor T-cell recognition
model_system: paired diagnosis/relapse primary AML samples and the corresponding patient-derived xenografts, profiled for gene expression, DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility; pharmacological PRC2 inhibition in vitro and in vivo
control_arm: vehicle-treated PDX and cultures; diagnosis-timepoint samples with intact HLA class II
mechanism: Loss of HLA class II at post-transplant relapse is enforced by PRC2-dependent closure of chromatin at the class II locus rather than by mutation, so an EZH2/PRC2 inhibitor can reopen it and restore surface expression.
key_finding: Class II loss tracked with PRC2-dependent reductions in chromatin accessibility, and PRC2 inhibitors restored HLA class II expression in relapsed AML both in vitro and in PDX models, with recovery of CD4+ T-cell recognition. Up to 40% of post-transplant relapses in this series were driven by nongenomic class II loss.
caveats: No approved myeloid PRC2 inhibitor and no such trial on this case's list, so the actionable read is diagnostic: measure HLA class II on the blasts before committing to a DLI- or graft-dependent strategy. Restoring recognition also restores graft-versus-host risk.

intervention_label: Myeloid sarcoma — site-specific clonal evolution and microenvironmental adaptation
model_system: paired myeloid sarcoma and medullary AML patient specimens profiled by multiomic sequencing, with matched circulating tumour DNA
control_arm: matched marrow AML from the same patients
mechanism: Extramedullary deposits arise from medullary AML but then evolve separately, acquiring RAS pathway activation and a transcriptional programme fitted to the soft-tissue microenvironment rather than the marrow niche.
key_finding: Myeloid sarcoma carried universal molecular evolution away from the marrow clone, with RAS pathway activation as a recurring hallmark and transcriptional signatures reflecting extramedullary adaptation. Circulating tumour DNA captured the molecular composition of the extramedullary lesion, which offers a non-invasive route to profiling a thigh mass.
caveats: Descriptive multiomics with no therapeutic arm, and antigen expression (CD33, CD123) was not the focus — so it establishes that marrow and thigh may diverge without saying by how much for the targets in play. Practical implication: biopsy or ctDNA-profile the thigh lesion rather than assuming the marrow panel represents it.

intervention_label: C1Q+ macrophage-like leukaemia subset driving extramedullary infiltration
model_system: single-cell RNA sequencing of paired bone marrow and extramedullary lesions, verified across multiple AML patients; patient-derived and cell-line-derived xenografts forming cutaneous and gastrointestinal nodules
control_arm: C1Q-low leukaemia populations; marrow-only disease; xenografts without MAFB-driven C1Q expression
mechanism: MAFB-driven C1Q expression gives blasts tissue-infiltration capacity; C1Q engages the globular C1Q receptor on fibroblasts, which release TGF-beta1 and both attract the blasts and protect them under chemotherapy stress.
key_finding: A C1Q+ macrophage-like subset was enriched in extramedullary lesions and detectable in marrow before extramedullary disease became clinically apparent, and it established cutaneous and gastrointestinal nodules in xenografts. Fibroblast crosstalk kept these cells alive under chemotherapy, which is a stromal explanation for sanctuary-site behaviour.
caveats: Anchored on one index patient with leukaemia cutis before broader verification, and skin/gut rather than deep soft tissue. No C1Q-directed agent exists, so the value is explanatory: an extramedullary deposit can be protected by stroma independently of the drug's target.

intervention_label: CD36-driven extramedullary dissemination and post-chemotherapy relapse
model_system: cohort of 1,273 AML patients for the expression-outcome association, plus xenograft mouse models with CD36 inhibition after chemotherapy
n_units: n=1,273 patients (association); xenograft arms for the intervention
control_arm: CD36-low blasts; untreated and chemotherapy-only xenograft arms
mechanism: CD36 acts here not as a lipid transporter but as a thrombospondin-1 receptor driving blast migration; CD36+ blasts adopt a senescence-like state that survives chemotherapy while retaining the ability to move into tissue.
key_finding: CD36 expression associated with extramedullary dissemination, higher relapse risk after intensive chemotherapy, and shorter event-free and overall survival. CD36+ blasts were enriched after chemotherapy, and CD36 inhibition reduced dissemination and prolonged survival in chemotherapy-treated xenografts.
caveats: Post-FLAG-IDA enrichment of a migratory, chemo-surviving population is a plausible account of how a thigh sarcoma appeared in this patient, but CD36 was not measured on her blasts and no CD36-directed agent is clinically available.
